stem: A fantasy lineup assistant uses a hand-written tool loop. Claude replies with three tool_use blocks at once: stats lookups for two running backs and an injury check for a tight end. The code runs the first call, returns its result, and the next API request fails. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Run all three calls and return the three tool_result blocks in one user message, matched by tool_use_id.
options.explanation: Correct. Every tool_use block in a turn needs a matching tool_result, and all of them belong in a single user message.

options.text: Disable parallel tool use for the session so Claude only ever asks for one tool call in each of its responses.
options.explanation: This hides the bug at the cost of slower, more numerous turns. The loop should handle parallel calls correctly instead.

options.text: Answer the first call only and drop the other two, since Claude will simply ask for them again on its next turn.
options.explanation: Unanswered tool_use blocks are exactly what makes the next request fail. Every call needs a result.

options.text: Send each of the three results back in its own user message, one after another, in the order the calls appeared.
options.explanation: Splitting results across messages is the wrong shape and teaches Claude to stop making parallel calls. Return them together.

stem: A game-day assistant calls an injury-feed tool that sometimes times out. When it does, the app throws an exception and the whole conversation ends with a generic error page. What should the tool loop do instead?

options.text: Retry the injury feed in a silent loop until it eventually succeeds, however long that takes to happen.
options.explanation: An unbounded silent retry can hang the conversation. Claude should learn about the failure and decide how to proceed.

options.text: Return a tool_result with is_error set to true and a clear message, so Claude can retry or change course.
options.explanation: Correct. Errors are results. A descriptive error lets Claude retry, use another source or tell the user, instead of the loop crashing.

options.text: Leave out the tool_result for the failed call, so that Claude doesn't see a confusing error in its context.
options.explanation: A tool_use block with no result makes the next request invalid. The failure must still be reported.

options.text: End the conversation and ask the user to start over once the injury feed is working normally again later.
options.explanation: This throws away the conversation for a recoverable failure. Claude can often finish the task without that one call.

stem: A report-writing agent's loop continues while stop_reason is tool_use and treats every other stop as a finished answer. Users report that long reports sometimes end mid-sentence with no error shown. What is the best change to the loop?

options.text: Add stop sequences to the request so the model always ends its report cleanly at a paragraph boundary.
options.explanation: Stop sequences end output earlier, not later. They can't prevent a response from being cut off by the token limit.

options.text: Treat any response that has no tool_use blocks in it as an end_turn, as the loop already does today.
options.explanation: That is the current bug. A response can stop for reasons other than finishing, and those need handling.

options.text: Branch on stop_reason: on max_tokens raise the limit or continue, and handle pause_turn and refusal too.
options.explanation: Correct. A max_tokens stop means the output was truncated. Each stop reason needs its own handling instead of being treated as success.

options.text: Lower the effort setting so that the model writes shorter reports that fit comfortably within the limit.
options.explanation: This might hide the symptom by degrading the reports, and the loop would still misreport any truncation that happens.

stem: A research agent uses the server-side web search tool. On long searches, some responses come back with stop_reason pause_turn, and the app shows those partial responses to users as final answers. How should the app handle pause_turn?

options.text: Discard the paused response and resend the original request from scratch to get a complete answer.
options.explanation: Starting over wastes the work already done and may pause again at the same point.

options.text: Treat it as a refusal and tell the user the request couldn't be completed because of a safety policy.
options.explanation: A refusal has its own stop reason. pause_turn means the turn paused, not that Claude declined.

options.text: Raise max_uses on the web search tool so that the search never needs to pause in the first place.
options.explanation: max_uses limits the number of searches. It doesn't stop a long server-tool turn from pausing.

options.text: Append the paused response to the conversation and send it back so that Claude can continue the turn.
options.explanation: Correct. pause_turn means a long server-tool turn paused. Sending the conversation back, including the paused content, lets Claude resume.

stem: A fantasy assistant serves thousands of users. In October, one coach says he never starts rookies in week 1; next September, in a brand-new conversation, the assistant should still know this, and other users must never see it. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Enable the memory tool and map /memories to per-user storage, so Claude saves the preference and reads it later.
options.explanation: Correct. The memory tool is for facts that must outlive a session. It is client-side, so the app scopes storage per user, and Claude checks memory before starting a task.

options.text: Add the preference to the project's CLAUDE.md, so that it loads automatically at the start of every session.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md holds stable project rules shared by every session. Writing one coach's preference there would expose it to all users.

options.text: Keep each coach's full season of chat history in the messages array and resend all of it with each request.
options.explanation: Replaying months of history bloats context and cost, and the new September conversation wouldn't have it anyway.

options.text: Resume the coach's October session by its session ID whenever he returns, so that its context is restored.
options.explanation: Resuming restores one conversation. It doesn't carry a fact into new conversations and drags the whole old transcript back in.

stem: A multi-tenant fan app adds the memory tool so its assistant can remember each fan's favorite team and past questions. Which TWO tasks are the app's responsibility? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Validate every path so operations stay under /memories and traversal such as ../ is rejected.
options.explanation: Correct. The app executes every file operation, so it must block paths that escape the memory directory.

options.text: Map /memories onto separate storage per fan, so that one fan's memory never reaches another.
options.explanation: Correct. /memories is a prefix your handler maps to real storage, so per-user isolation is the app's job.

options.text: Nothing beyond enabling the tool, because Anthropic stores memory files server-side for the app.
options.explanation: The memory tool is client-side. Claude only requests operations; the app executes and stores them.

options.text: Add a system prompt rule telling Claude to always view its memory directory before anything else.
options.explanation: The API adds that memory protocol to the system prompt automatically when the tool is present.

options.text: Turn off context editing, because clearing old tool results can't be combined with the memory tool.
options.explanation: The two are designed to work together. Claude gets a warning to save important information before results are cleared.

stem: A logistics team is building a claims-processing agent. It mixes fixed code steps with LLM steps, must resume where it left off after a server crash, and needs to pause so a human can inspect and edit its state before a payment step. Which framework's core design matches this best?

options.text: Pydantic AI, because its main strength is validating structured outputs against typed Python models.
options.explanation: Typed, validated outputs are useful, but the stated needs are explicit control flow, durable execution and human-in-the-loop pauses.

options.text: LangGraph, because it models stateful graphs with durable execution and human-in-the-loop interrupts.
options.explanation: Correct. LangGraph is a low-level orchestration runtime for long-running, stateful agents, with durable execution and pauses for human inspection.

options.text: Strands Agents, because its model-driven loop lets the model decide each step without any fixed path.
options.explanation: A model-driven loop is the opposite of what's wanted here. The team needs explicit, deterministic steps mixed with LLM steps.

options.text: A single Messages API call with a long prompt that describes every step, crash recovery and the pause.
options.explanation: One call can't persist state across a crash or wait for a human. Those need an orchestration layer.

stem: A Python team's scouting tool must return player evaluations as validated, typed objects, re-prompting the model automatically when validation fails. The team also wants to inject a database connection into tools so tests can swap in a fake. Which framework fits this priority best?

options.text: LangGraph, because a graph of nodes and edges is the only way to validate structured agent output.
options.explanation: LangGraph focuses on orchestration and state. Graphs aren't required for output validation.

options.text: Strands Agents, because its swarm pattern lets several agents cross-check each other's evaluations.
options.explanation: Multi-agent cross-checking adds cost and doesn't give typed, schema-validated objects or dependency injection.

options.text: Pydantic AI, because it returns validated typed outputs and injects dependencies into tools.
options.explanation: Correct. Pydantic AI validates runs against an output type, retries on validation failure and has type-safe dependency injection.

options.text: No framework at all, just a manual loop with regular expressions that parse the model's text.
options.explanation: Regex parsing is brittle, and the team would rebuild validation, retries and injection by hand.

stem: A media company wants to give an agent a model, a system prompt and a set of tools, and let the model plan its own steps. It also wants built-in multi-agent patterns such as agents-as-tools and swarms, MCP support, and the freedom to switch between providers such as Anthropic and Amazon Bedrock. Which option matches this best?

options.text: LangGraph, where the team defines every node and edge of the agent's control flow up front.
options.explanation: LangGraph gives explicit control flow you design. The company wants the model to plan its own steps.

options.text: Pydantic AI, where the main design goal is typed outputs that are validated against schemas.
options.explanation: Pydantic AI is model-agnostic, but its focus is typed outputs. The stated priorities are a model-driven loop and multi-agent patterns.

options.text: A hand-written Messages API loop, with multi-agent patterns and MCP support written in-house.
options.explanation: Possible, but the team would rebuild what it explicitly wants supplied, including multi-agent wiring and provider switching.

options.text: Strands Agents, an open-source SDK built around a model-driven loop and multi-agent patterns.
options.explanation: Correct. Strands describes itself as a model-driven approach, with built-in MCP, multi-agent patterns and first-class support for providers including Anthropic and Bedrock.

stem: An analyst has an Agent SDK session in which a scouting agent has already reviewed a quarterback's film. She wants to try a different evaluation approach from that point while keeping the original session intact for comparison. Which option fits best?

options.text: Fork the session, which branches a copy from that point and leaves the original session unchanged.
options.explanation: Correct. Forking branches into a different approach without modifying the original, and both keep the earlier context.

options.text: Resume the original session with the new approach, then undo any changes if the result is worse.
options.explanation: Resuming continues and changes the original session, which she wants to keep intact for comparison.

options.text: Start a fresh session and paste in a short summary of the film review that was done in the first one.
options.explanation: A pasted summary loses the detail of the earlier work, so the comparison would not start from the same point.

options.text: Save the film review to the memory tool and load it from there in every later analysis session.
options.explanation: Memory is for durable facts across sessions, not for branching an in-progress conversation.

stem: In a hand-written loop, a draft assistant exposes a research_player tool that runs its own sub-agent loop with separate messages and tools. That sub-loop reads dozens of scouting reports per call. What should research_player return to the parent agent?

options.text: The sub-loop's full transcript, including every report it read, so the parent can check its work.
options.explanation: This puts all the reports into the parent's context, which is exactly what the sub-agent was meant to prevent.

options.text: A short final report as the tool_result, while the sub-loop's own history stays inside the sub-agent.
options.explanation: Correct. In the agents-as-tools pattern, the parent sends a self-contained task and gets back a concise report. Noisy work stays in the sub-agent.

options.text: Nothing at all, because the sub-loop appends its messages directly to the parent's messages array.
options.explanation: Sharing one messages array removes the isolation and mixes two conversations' tool blocks together.

options.text: An empty tool_result, after the sub-loop writes its findings into a global variable the parent reads.
options.explanation: Hidden side channels make the loop hard to debug, and Claude doesn't see the findings in its context.

stem: A developer's manual loop appends only the text from each assistant response to the history, then appends the tool results in the next user message. The API rejects the follow-up request. What is wrong?

options.text: Tool results must be sent with the assistant role, because the assistant was the one that asked for them.
options.explanation: Tool results go in a user message. The role is right; the preceding assistant message is incomplete.

options.text: The loop needs a turn cap. Without one the API rejects any request that contains a tool_result block.
options.explanation: A turn cap is good practice, but the API doesn't require it. The rejection comes from the history's shape.

options.text: The full assistant content must be appended, because tool_result blocks refer to tool_use blocks in it.
options.explanation: Correct. Each tool_result points at a tool_use_id. If the tool_use blocks were stripped from the history, the results have nothing to match.

options.text: Tool results must be wrapped as text in the system prompt, because the API only reads tool data there.
options.explanation: Tool results are tool_result content blocks in the user turn. The system prompt is for instructions.

stem: A league office wants a research agent that works on a rules study for a week. The process may restart at any time, the agent should resume the next day from where it stopped, and its working context should stay small throughout. Which combination fits best?

options.text: Compaction alone, because its summary is stored server-side and is reloaded on its own after a restart.
options.explanation: The API is stateless. Compaction keeps a conversation small, but the app holds the history, and nothing reloads it after a restart.

options.text: One long conversation on a 1M-token model, so that the whole week of work fits inside a single window.
options.explanation: A large window doesn't survive a process restart, and quality degrades as a week of tool output piles up.

options.text: Subagents for every step, since each one starts fresh and the parent can rebuild the state from them.
options.explanation: Subagents isolate context within a run, but they don't persist anything across restarts or days.

options.text: A memory-tool progress file read at startup, plus context editing or compaction within each session.
options.explanation: Correct. Memory persists state across restarts and sessions, while context editing or compaction keep the working window small. Long-running agents often use both.

stem: In one turn, a roster agent's custom loop receives five tool_use blocks: three get_stats lookups, which are read-only, and two update_roster calls that change league data. Which TWO handling choices are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run the three read-only get_stats lookups concurrently, because they don't change any shared state.
options.explanation: Correct. Independent read-only calls are safe to run in parallel, which shortens the turn.

options.text: Run the two roster updates one after another, then send all five results in one user message.
options.explanation: Correct. State-changing calls run sequentially to avoid conflicts, and every result for the turn goes back together.

options.text: Send each result back as soon as its call finishes, each one in a separate user message.
options.explanation: All results for one assistant turn belong in a single user message.

options.text: Skip the second roster update if it looks like the first, and send no tool_result for it.
options.explanation: Every tool_use needs a result. If a call is rejected, return that as an error result instead of dropping it.

options.text: Set tool_choice to any on the next request, so Claude makes only one tool call per turn.
options.explanation: Forcing tool_choice doesn't limit calls to one, and current models reject forced tool_choice anyway.

stem: An architect at a ticketing company is deciding whether to build a two-tool order-lookup agent on an agent framework or directly on the Claude API. Which TWO statements reflect Anthropic's guidance? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Many agent patterns take only a few lines on the API, so start there and add a framework when it earns its place.
options.explanation: Correct. Anthropic recommends starting with the API directly, since a simple loop is often enough.

options.text: If a framework is used, the team should understand the prompts and responses it produces underneath.
options.explanation: Correct. Abstraction layers can hide prompts and responses, which makes debugging harder unless the team knows what is underneath.

options.text: Frameworks always make agents more reliable, because they add retries and validation automatically.
options.explanation: Frameworks can add useful features, but extra layers also add complexity and can obscure failures. It isn't automatic.

options.text: Pick the framework with the largest community, since popularity is the best predictor of a good fit.
options.explanation: Fit depends on matching the framework's abstraction to the problem, not on popularity.

options.text: A framework removes the need to design tool names, descriptions and outputs carefully for the agent.
options.explanation: Tool design matters whatever runs the loop. A framework doesn't write good tool descriptions for you.

stem: A hand-written agent loop keeps calling Claude while `stop_reason` is `tool_use`. Now and then a research task gets stuck calling the same search tool more than 200 times, running up a large bill before anyone notices. Which safeguard belongs in the loop?

options.text: Remove the search tool so Claude can only answer from what it already knows
options.explanation: This breaks the feature for every task to stop a rare runaway. The loop itself needs a limit.

options.text: Add a system-prompt line asking Claude not to search more than necessary
options.explanation: An instruction may reduce the problem, but it doesn't put a hard bound on turns or spend.

options.text: Cap turns (and ideally spend), stopping with a clear status when the cap is hit
options.explanation: Correct. A hard cap in code bounds the worst case whatever the model does, and a clear status lets the app report or escalate the unfinished task.

options.text: Lower `max_tokens` so each turn in the loop costs less
options.explanation: Cheaper turns don't stop an unbounded number of them, and a low cap can truncate useful responses.

stem: A team built its scouting agent on an agent framework. The agent sometimes ignores a rule the team is sure it wrote, but the developers can't see the exact prompt and tool definitions the framework sends to Claude. Which response best follows Anthropic's guidance?

options.text: Inspect the raw requests and responses the framework produces, and learn how it builds them
options.explanation: Correct. Anthropic's guidance is that if you use a framework, you must understand the underlying code. Seeing the real prompt is the first step to finding why the rule is lost.

options.text: Repeat the rule in several places in the framework's configuration until the agent follows it
options.explanation: Without seeing what is actually sent, this is guesswork and may make the prompt worse.

options.text: Switch to a different framework with more built-in agent patterns
options.explanation: More abstraction doesn't address the real problem, which is that the team can't see what Claude receives.

options.text: Move to a larger model, which is better at following rules hidden deep in long prompts
options.explanation: The rule may not be in the prompt at all. Changing models without looking at the request treats a symptom.

stem: A recap agent built with the Agent SDK must always use the league's approved team abbreviations. The rule is known in advance and never changes. A developer proposes storing it with the memory tool so the agent can "remember" it. Where should the rule live?

options.text: In the memory tool's `/memories` directory, so Claude can choose to read it when needed
options.explanation: The memory tool suits facts the agent learns over time. A fixed rule shouldn't depend on Claude deciding to look it up.

options.text: In the first user message of each session, so it is close to the task
options.explanation: A first message can be summarized away by compaction in long sessions, and it depends on every caller remembering to include it.

options.text: In a database the recap tool queries whenever it writes a team name
options.explanation: That's possible for the data itself, but the instruction to use the abbreviations still has to reach Claude every time.

options.text: In the system prompt or CLAUDE.md, where stable rules are supplied with every request
options.explanation: Correct. Rules that are known up front and always apply belong where they are loaded every time. Long-term memory is for what the agent learns.

stem: A parent agent has spent twenty turns with a GM discussing a trade for a backup quarterback named in the conversation. It then delegates to a sub-agent with the task "check his injury history". The sub-agent reports on the wrong player. Which fix best fits?

options.text: Give the sub-agent read access to the parent's full message history
options.explanation: This defeats the purpose of a sub-agent, which is to work in a small, separate context.

options.text: Send a self-contained task naming the player, his ID and what the GM needs to know
options.explanation: Correct. A sub-agent has its own history and sees only what it is sent. The delegation must carry everything needed to do the task.

options.text: Switch the sub-agent to a more capable model so it can infer which player is meant
options.explanation: No model can recover information it was never given. The brief itself is incomplete.

options.text: Stop using sub-agents and have the parent read all injury reports itself
options.explanation: This gives up the context isolation sub-agents provide, when the actual fix is a better brief.
